A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FairLocator study. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of four VLMs, a human study, and experiments involving temporal imagery, author-provided photographs, and Chinatown scenes.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical results and adds entropy and distance measurements, sample-size and rural evaluations, a prompting comparison, and an o3 case study.

M1.justification: The main geolocation prompt, JSON outputs, EXIF removal, retry procedure, and exact/GPT-4o semantic matching remain unchanged. Direct prompting is introduced as an experimental comparator, without replacing the main procedure or introducing a new model architecture.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds evaluation on five explicitly rural U.S. locations, including Woodstock and Smicksburg, extending beyond v1's illustrative rural-looking scenes. The original global benchmark, temporal imagery, author photographs, and Chinatown coverage remain. Increased image counts and selection of existing failures do not independently expand task coverage.

E2.justification: The main four-model comparison and human comparator are retained. Appendix F newly compares Gemini with and without CoT prompting, while Appendix G evaluates o3 on cases that GPT-4o misclassified. These are limited supplementary comparator additions, not an expansion of every benchmark comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds entropy and geodesic error-distance evaluation, including country-area normalization and a 20,015 km penalty for unknown cities. New protocols examine 20 versus 10 images, rural versus urban locations, direct prompting, and GPT-4o-selected failures. Section 3.1 also changes the reported coordinate source from Simplemaps to Google Geocoding. These changes do not establish that the original benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices D–G substantially expand diagnostics through sample-size sensitivity, quantitative rural–urban comparison, CoT ablation, and o3 failure cases. Section 5.1 also adds observations about changing buildings at three Las Vegas locations. The original CoT examples are retained in Appendix F, rather than newly introduced, and existing Chinatown and visual-style analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix D newly reports variability statistics, described as mean standard deviations of city-level accuracy: 0.406 with 20 images and 0.370 with 10. Appendices D and E specify single-query experiments, while the original three-response protocol remains. The new variability reporting does not establish repeated-run uncertainty or introduce confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: All five original accuracy tables retain their numerical values after matching. v2 adds entropy and distance tables, per-model temporal results, sample-size accuracies of 63.0% versus 64.8%, CoT versus direct-prompt accuracies of 63.0% versus 61.0%, rural versus urban results of 3% versus 57.7%, and 0% for o3 on selected failures. These are substantial added outcomes, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 introduces limited mathematical scoring definitions, particularly error distance divided by the square root of country land area, alongside normalized prediction entropy and its stated 0–1 range. Neither version develops theoretical propositions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The benchmark contribution, claim to first expose VLM geolocation biases, principal bias patterns, and privacy warning retain their meaning and scope. Entropy and distance findings provide additional support. Renaming the framework and dataset as a benchmark and compressing the conclusion do not establish a different core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 newly argues that ten images are sufficient, links rural failures to population density and visual distinctiveness, and suggests similar biases in o3. Temporal-error interpretation emphasizes changing visual features, and the privacy discussion explicitly extends risks beyond populous cities. The principal training-imbalance hypothesis and stated Limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 3.1 newly describes random nearby coordinates and viewing angles and identifies Google Geocoding as the coordinate source. New experiments include sampling and query details. Conversely, Section 5.1 drops v1's explicit identical-location control and ten-locations-per-city, 90-image description, without establishing that those controls were abandoned. Code and dataset access disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Luo et al. (2025) on geolocation privacy, Shi et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2024) when distinguishing spatial reasoning from city geolocation, and Shannon (1948) for entropy. Existing related-work summaries are compressed, but the central positioning around previously unexamined geolocation biases remains.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites affect the abstract, related work, results discussion, conclusion, and privacy statement. Section 3 becomes Data and Metrics in FairLocator, and the CoT discussion moves from Section 5.3 to Appendix F. The principal section sequence and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds three metric tables and two illustrated o3 examples. The original depth-accuracy table moves from the main text to an enlarged Appendix A table, while CoT panels move to the appendix and existing plots are rearranged. This substantially changes the distribution and presentation of evidence, although every original graphic is retained.

improvement.justification: Explicit entropy and distance measurements make the bias evaluation more informative, and the quantitative prompting comparison strengthens v1's illustrative CoT discussion. These gains are limited by reporting problems: the conclusion assigns entropy near 0.54 to Brazil despite Table 1, and Appendix E's percentages do not align with its stated single-query sample counts. Temporal sample and matching details are also lost. The retained original evidence and useful additional diagnostics support a limited net improvement.
